extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of American political institutions; scholars of legislative procedure; general readers interested in Congress
extracted.subtask_description: Analytic criteria for assessing the quality, openness, and political significance of debates and committee government in the U.S. House of Representatives (institutional/political-science perspective).

rubrics_metrics.name: Public, high‑stakes legislative discussion
rubrics_metrics.description: For the instruction and elevation of public opinion there is needed something more than special pleas for special privileges. There is needed public discussion ... by the sovereign legislative body itself ... every feature of each mooted point of policy shall be distinctly brought out, and every argument of significance pushed to the farthest point of insistence, by recognized leaders in that body; and, above all, a discussion upon which something — something of interest or importance ... evidently depends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only debates that are public, full, led by recognized leaders, and visibly consequential (party fortunes, administration, important law) will engage and instruct the public. Debates lacking stakes or leadership will not be heeded; committee pleas and special-pleader arguments are insufficient. Example/anti-pattern: lengthy committee orations with no party stakes fail to inform the citizenry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Committee secrecy and control over disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Committees are privileged and accustomed to hold their sessions in absolute secrecy. It is made a breach of order for any member to allude on the floor of the House to anything that has taken place in committee, 'unless by a written report sanctioned by a majority of the Committee.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Secrecy constrains public debate and limits the usefulness of committee proceedings to the public. The text notes that arguments are only heard before committees by concession; committees control what becomes public via sanctioned written reports. Anti-pattern: committee deliberations kept secret while the public expects transparent legislative reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chamber physical layout supporting effective debate
rubrics_metrics.description: Physical and architectural reasons make business-like debate in the House out of the question: the chamber is immense, with roomy desks, broad aisles, deep galleries, and much noise — a speaker must have an exceptional voice to command attention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Architecture and acoustics matter: a hall that disperses members and permits noise undermines sustained, searching debate. The author suggests remedies (e.g., dividing into a smaller debating hall and a larger reading-room). Scoring could consider whether a chamber's design facilitates close exchange, attention, and orderly debate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticity of printed debates
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress is constantly granting leave to its members to insert in the official reports of the proceedings speeches which it never heard and does not care to hear, but which it is not averse from printing at the public expense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Published 'debates' (Congressional Record) may include statements not actually delivered; this undermines the Record as a faithful account. Evaluation should check whether printed speeches reflect actual floor delivery or are post-hoc insertions intended for constituents. Anti-pattern: assuming printed text equals spoken debate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concentration of leadership and clear party responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: There are in Congress no authoritative leaders who are the recognized spokesmen of their parties. Power is scattered amongst many small chiefs ... The less a man has to do — the more he is confined to single departments — the more intelligent and thorough will his work be. Yet the more power is divided the more irresponsible it becomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Meaningful, public, partisan debate requires concentrated, accountable leadership (as in parliamentary ministries). Absence of recognized national party leaders within Congress diffuses responsibility and weakens the connection between debate and electoral accountability. Evaluation should consider existence and clarity of party leadership and whether leaders carry responsibility visibly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Committee composition's effect on partisan accountability
rubrics_metrics.description: Committee reports ... represent merely the recommendations of a small body of members belonging to both parties ... The manifest object is to dress them to the liking of all factions. Under such circumstances, neither the failure nor the success of any policy inaugurated by one of the Committees can fairly be charged to the account of either party.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mixed-party committee make-ups tend to produce neutral, compromise reports that blur party responsibility. For accountability and clear party debate, committees composed primarily of the majority (party) would produce party-backed reports and clearer opposition/majority contest. Assessment should examine committee composition and how it affects visibility of party positions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural rules and time pressure limiting deliberation
rubrics_metrics.description: The rules then simply served and did not tyrannize over the House. They did not then have the opportunity of empire afforded them by the scantiness of time which hurries the House, and the weight of business which oppresses it ... nowadays would-be debaters are easily thrust out of Congress and forced to resort to the printing-office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: How rules (use of previous question, limits on debate) and calendar pressure truncate meaningful discussion. Evaluation should consider whether procedural rules facilitate or stifle searching debate and whether time constraints push speech-making into printed rather than oral venues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Debate must carry immediate, tangible stakes to engage the public
rubrics_metrics.description: The ordinary citizen cannot be induced to pay much heed ... unless something else more interesting than the law itself be involved in the pending decision ... If the fortunes of a party or the power of a great political leader are staked upon the final vote, he will listen with the keenest interest ... but if no such things hang in the balance, he will not turn from his business to listen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public attention and instructional value of debate correlate with perceived stakes (party fortunes, leadership). Evaluators should look for whether debates are structured and framed so that the public recognizes consequential choices; absent stakes, even accurate debate will attract little readership or engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Speaker's committee appointment power and its political consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: The Speaker's privilege of appointing the Standing Committees of the House ... that power is, as it were, the central and characteristic inconvenience and anomaly of our constitutional system ... he who appoints those Committees is an autocrat of the first magnitude.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The mechanism for appointing committees centralizes influence in the Speaker; the identity and disposition of the Speaker materially shape legislative outcomes. Evaluation should note appointment rules, variation with individual Speakers, and the resulting political weight and potential for partisan control or patronage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislation should be an expression of party policy for electoral accountability
rubrics_metrics.description: It seems unquestionably and in a high degree desirable that all legislation should distinctly represent the action of parties as parties ... so that the voters might be able to declare by their ballots ... their condemnation of any past policy ... and also their will as to the future administration of the government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For democratic accountability, laws and votes should translate into recognizable party platforms/actions that voters can reward or punish. Assessment should check whether legislative outputs map onto party responsibility or are aggregates of mixed-committee compromises that obscure electoral choice.
